nodes.description: The standard intervention for severe-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss, and the only one with any DFNB35-relevant outcome data. That data is thin and should not be overstated: in a study designed to find genetic causes of *poor* implant outcome, an ESRRB variant appeared among the matched controls with good outcomes rather than among the cases, alongside five other genes. A single ESRRB child also appears in a series of genetically characterised implant candidates undergoing vestibular testing. Neither study reports ESRRB-specific implant performance, and neither has a DFNB35 denominator.

nodes.description: Biallelic ESRRB alleles that reduce or abolish the transcriptional output of ERR-beta. The reported spectrum is dominated by missense substitutions: of the coding variants described to date, all but one lie in the DNA-binding domain or the ligand-binding domain, split roughly evenly between them. Truncating alleles exist but are the minority - the seven base pair exon 8 duplication that defined the gene in the Turkish family, and a canonical donor splice variant that skips exon 4 and triggers nonsense-mediated decay. Because most alleles are missense, DFNB35 is better read as a graded loss of transcription factor activity than as a clean null.

nodes.description: ERR-beta is expressed specifically in the endolymph-producing cells of the inner ear - strial marginal cells in the cochlea, vestibular dark cells in the ampulla and utricle - and controls their development. Without it, these cells fail to express the panel of ion channel and transporter genes that makes them secretory, and they partially convert toward the identity of the adjacent Pendrin-expressing epithelium. This is a cell-fate defect, which is a different lesion from the transport defects that Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (KCNQ1, KCNE1) or Delpire-McNeill syndrome (SLC12A2) produce in the same cells: there the machinery is installed and broken, here it is not installed.

nodes.description: The tissue-level consequence: an endolymph-secreting epithelium that cannot secrete. In the mosaic mouse the defect is not confined to the marginal cell layer - null marginal cells alter gene expression in the intermediate cells beneath them and the local strial capillary bed is lost, so the stria fails as a three-layer unit rather than as one cell type. Both the endocochlear potential and the endolymphatic potassium concentration depend on this epithelium, and lesions elsewhere in the same compartment are established causes of profound deafness. Graded PROVISIONAL because the endolymph and endocochlear potential consequences of ESRRB loss specifically have not been measured; what is measured is the loss of the machinery that produces them.

nodes.description: The finding that makes "nonsyndromic" arguable. In the two DFNB35 families examined for it - the Turkish exon 8 duplication family and the Czech p.R291L family - dental destruction by caries was markedly more extensive in mutation carriers than in unaffected relatives. This is not classical syndromic deafness: there is no enamel dysplasia, no other organ system involved, and the observation rests on two families plus locus-level association data from unrelated caries cohorts.

nodes.description: The molecular consequence measured directly in patient material and in inner-ear derived cells. The recurrent p.Arg382Cys ligand-binding-domain substitution does not stop ERR-beta reaching the nucleus - subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemistry show wild-type-like nuclear localisation - but it destabilises the protein and abolishes its activity on a reporter promoter. Downstream, transcripts of ESRRB target genes fall by roughly half in patient-derived lymphoblastoid lines, including ATP1B1, which encodes the Na+/K+-ATPase beta-1 subunit that inner ear ion gradients depend on. The distinction matters mechanistically: this is a transcriptional output failure, not a trafficking failure.

nodes.description: A second, non-cochlear site of ESRRB action that complicates the "nonsyndromic" label. Esrrb protein is present in mouse ameloblasts during the secretory stage of amelogenesis, when enamel matrix is laid down, but not at the later maturation stage. The proposed consequence is enamel that is more susceptible to acid dissolution rather than a recognisable enamel dysplasia, which is consistent with the clinical picture being excess caries rather than amelogenesis imperfecta. This is curated as a modifier node, not as part of the hearing loss chain.
